title: The pharmacology of cocaethylene in humans following cocaine and ethanol administration

claims.statement: In one double-blind laboratory study of 8 adults who were already using cocaine and alcohol together, adding alcohol to repeated cocaine doses was associated with a higher heart rate, roughly 13% to 15% more cocaine in the blood over the session, and cocaethylene, a substance the body makes only when both drugs are present. In 8-hour inpatient sessions, with four nasal cocaine doses 30 minutes apart (1 mg per kg each) and oral alcohol dosed to hold the blood level near 100 mg/dL (study conditions, not amounts to use), heart rate was higher with the combination than with cocaine alone (p = .002; about 84 against 74 beats a minute averaged over the session, an editors' calculation from the printed areas under the curve). Cocaine exposure was higher with alcohol (p = .035), and cocaethylene, never found with either drug alone, cleared more slowly than cocaine (half-life 156 against 85 minutes). People rated feeling good more highly with the combination than with cocaine alone (p = .04) but did not rate any high significantly higher (p = .09), and blood pressure did not differ detectably from cocaine alone; blood alcohol was lower with cocaine (99 against 118 mg/dL at the one time point reported). A narrative review of 14 small laboratory studies, which includes this one, describes second-hand up to 30% more blood cocaine, cocaethylene only with both drugs, and heart-rate rises that were additive with a trend towards greater than additive; it also describes one 6-person study in which alcohol came 30 minutes after cocaine and blood cocaine did not rise. The review adds that no retrospective study it covers shows unequivocally that the combination harms the heart more, and that one emergency-room study of over 1,000 patients found no more cardiovascular problems in people positive for both drugs than for one. The study had 8 people, gave cocaine by the nose to people who usually smoked it, and counted p below .05 one-tailed as significant across 15 measures without correction, so the heart-rate result is the sturdiest and the cocaine-exposure and feel-good results would not reach .05 on a two-tailed test (an editors' calculation). It reports no heart events or rhythm findings, cannot say whether the heart-rate rise came from the extra cocaine or from cocaethylene, and cannot show what happens outside a ward. In a second double-blind laboratory study, 10 adults who used cocaine and alcohol (8 men and 2 women, mean age 34, none of whom had sought treatment for cocaine problems) drank alcohol (1 g per kg) an hour before cocaine was infused into a vein over 15 minutes, in four sessions with labelled cocaine at 0.3, 0.6 or 1.2 mg per kg or a cocaine placebo and one double-placebo session (study conditions, not amounts to use): about 17% of the cocaine dose (SD 6) appeared as cocaethylene, in the same proportion across the four-fold dose range, and cocaethylene peaked later than cocaine and at far lower levels (16.8 to 53.1 against 250 to 891 ng/mL). None was found when cocaine was given without alcohol. With alcohol present, less benzoylecgonine, the breakdown product urine tests look for, was formed and excreted (peak blood level 69% and urine concentration about half of the cocaine-alone values). In those sessions, unlike the intranasal studies, alcohol did not raise cocaine exposure: in the 6 people who later also had a cocaine-alone session, cocaine exposure over the session and its peak did not differ, although cocaine's half-life was longer with alcohol (1.91 against 1.29 hours), and they rated drug liking and total intoxication higher across time, but not at their peak, with alcohol than with cocaine alone. That cocaine-alone session was neither blinded nor randomized and came 1 to 3 months later, in 6 of the 10 people, and a tracer dose of labelled cocaethylene was given in every session, so no session was free of cocaethylene (Harris et al., 2003). When cocaethylene itself was infused into a vein at the same doses as cocaine (0.25 and 0.5 mg per kg) in 6 adults with cocaine dependence who also met criteria for alcohol abuse or dependence, each taking all five conditions double-blind with placebo, it raised heart rate less than cocaine and produced lower ratings of cocaine high, any high, rush and feeling stimulated, while systolic blood pressure rose about equally in all four active conditions and diastolic pressure showed no difference; cocaethylene was cleared more slowly (half-life about 146 to 149 against 87 to 91 minutes). The lower dose of each drug was always given before the higher one, so dose and session order are mixed together, and the blind held poorly at the lower doses: given cocaine at 0.25 mg per kg, 5 of the 6 said they had been given cocaethylene (Hart et al., 2000). Cocaethylene is found in people's blood after combined use: in 7 post-mortem samples, sent to a laboratory because peaks suggesting cocaethylene had already been seen in them, it ran from 73 to 1447 ng/mL and exceeded cocaine in 4; among emergency-department samples, 10 of 17 that contained a cocaine breakdown product and alcohol held cocaethylene, against 1 of 14 that contained cocaine but no alcohol, and incubation tests showed that it does not form in a sample after collection. Those 7 deaths have no stated cause, no comparison deaths and no denominator, so they show presence, never cause (Jatlow et al., 1991). The three studies added here do not settle what cocaethylene contributes either: given on its own it was less potent than cocaine at matched doses, and when it is formed in the body its levels stay well below cocaine's, but no study gave it at the levels combined use produces, and none of these studies measured a heart event, a rhythm problem or any other harm.
claims.magnitude: McCance-Katz et al. (1998), combination against cocaine alone: heart rate p = .002 (areas under the curve over 480 minutes 40,289 (SEM 940) against 35,658 (647); editors' calculation, averages of about 83.9 against 74.3 beats per minute; alcohol alone 34,778 (933), about 72.5). Blood pressure: no significant difference from cocaine alone; the combination was higher than alcohol alone (systolic p = .008, diastolic p = .003). Cocaine: peak 893 (SEM 114) against 754 (114) ng/mL; area under the curve 153,562 (19,489) against 135,371 (19,892) ng x min/mL, described as about 15% greater (editors' calculation from the printed means: 13.4%), p = .035; half-life 85 against 83 minutes. Cocaethylene, only with the combination: half-life 156 (15.3) minutes, longer than cocaine (p = .001); peak 114 (18) ng/mL at 180 minutes; its area under the curve is 0.20 of cocaine's. Ratings: feel good higher than with cocaine alone (p = .04, peak at 120 minutes); any high p = .09; rush, sleepy, paranoid, crash, sad or depressed and desire for cocaine not significantly different (no values printed). Blood alcohol lower with the combination (p = .008, data not shown; 99 (SE 7) against 118 (10) mg/dL 30 minutes after the second alcohol dose). The paper counts p below .05 one-tailed as significant across 15 measures without correction; doubling the p values (editors' calculation) gives about .07 for cocaine exposure and .08 for feel good. Pennings et al. (2002), second-hand: blood cocaine up to 30% higher when cocaine came with or after alcohol (5 studies, this one among them); cocaethylene only with both drugs (6 studies); blood alcohol unchanged in 1 study and about 10% lower, not significantly, in 4; heart rate additive with a trend towards greater than additive; one 6-person study with alcohol 30 minutes after cocaine: heart-rate rises additive and no rise in blood cocaine; in over 1,000 emergency-room screens, no more cardiovascular problems in people positive for both drugs than for one. Harris et al. (2003), 10 adults, alcohol 1 g/kg an hour before intravenous cocaine: cocaethylene formed from 17% (SD 6) of the cocaine dose (1.8 mg of cocaethylene per 10 mg of cocaine, range 1.0 to 4.0), with no difference between the 0.3, 0.6 and 1.2 mg/kg doses; cocaethylene peak 16.8 (SD 7.64), 30.1 (11.1) and 53.1 (15.0) ng/mL against cocaine peaks of 250 (73.0), 438 (151) and 891 (271) ng/mL; cocaethylene peaked at 1.31 to 1.55 hours against 0.28 to 0.36 hours for cocaine, with half-lives of about 2.5 and 1.8 hours; no cocaethylene was detectable in the cocaine-only condition. In the 6 people tested both ways (1.2 mg/kg): cocaine exposure 1030 against 1010 h·ng/mL and peak 968 against 823 ng/mL, neither different; cocaine half-life 1.91 (0.51) against 1.29 (0.15) hours, P < 0.02; peak blood benzoylecgonine 452 (62.2) against 652 (111) ng/mL, P < 0.01; urine benzoylecgonine concentration 7770 against 14 800 ng/mL, P < 0.02; higher ratings across time of total intoxication (P < 0.02) and drug liking (P < 0.04) and a higher heart rate across time (P < 0.05) with alcohol, with no difference in peak ratings, peak heart rate, blood pressure or rate-pressure product. Hart et al. (2000), 6 adults, cocaethylene against cocaine at 0.25 and 0.5 mg/kg into a vein: condition effect on heart rate F = 12.37, P < 0.01, with cocaine 0.5 mg/kg above every other active condition and no difference between cocaine 0.25 mg/kg and either cocaethylene dose; ratings 2.5 minutes after dosing (0 to 100), placebo, cocaine 0.25 and 0.5, cocaethylene 0.25 and 0.5: cocaine high 10, 44.2, 65.3, 15.3, 41.7; rush 5, 47.5, 68.8, 13.3, 34.6; half-life 149 (SE 11.07) and 146 (9.49) minutes for cocaethylene against 91 (9.01) and 87 (7.19) for cocaine; systolic pressure raised above placebo in all four active conditions with no difference between them. Jatlow et al. (1991): cocaethylene 73 to 1447 ng/mL in 7 selected post-mortem samples, alongside cocaine 34 to 4370 ng/mL and alcohol 20 to 240 mg/dL, exceeding cocaine in 4 of the 7; cocaethylene in 10 of 17 emergency-department samples with a cocaine breakdown product and alcohol, and in 1 of 14 with cocaine but no alcohol.

claims.statement: In one double-blind laboratory study now read in full, and in a narrative review of 14 small laboratory studies whose own primary studies have not been read here, people given cocaine with alcohol did not rate themselves as more drunk than with alcohol alone. In the study read in full, 10 adults who used cocaine and alcohol drank alcohol (1 g per kg; study conditions only) an hour before cocaine was infused into a vein over 15 minutes, in four double-blind sessions with cocaine at 0.3, 0.6 or 1.2 mg per kg or a cocaine placebo, and one double-placebo session: their ratings of alcohol intoxication peaked 55 minutes after the first drink, 5 minutes before the infusion began, and did not differ between sessions, whatever cocaine dose followed, while breath alcohol peaked at 0.12 g/dL or above in every session with alcohol. Because the alcohol was drunk an hour before the cocaine, its peak was reached before any cocaine arrived (Harris et al., 2003). As described second-hand by the review: in three studies cocaine produced a slight decrease in rated drunkenness (the review's table calls the fall non-significant in two of them) and in one it had no effect, while ratings of the cocaine high, or of global intoxication, were greater in six studies when alcohol came before or with the cocaine (in one of the six, the multiple-dose study read in full, the rise in rated any high fell short of significance, p = .09). Cocaine also lessened some alcohol-related deficits on laboratory tests (digit-symbol substitution, sedation, learning and psychomotor tasks), and blood alcohol with cocaine was unchanged in one study and about 10% lower, not significantly, in four. In the multiple-dose study, blood alcohol was lower with cocaine (99 against 118 mg/dL at one time point), no rating of drunkenness was reported, and a rating of feeling sleepy did not differ. The same review reports that 21 of 600 fatally injured drivers in Los Angeles County and 12 of 285 in Spain tested positive for both drugs, which it reads as no definitive protection from the impairing effects of alcohol, and it describes no study that asked other people how drunk someone who had taken both appeared. The laboratory studies had 6 to 34 people each (13 of the 14 had 12 or fewer), and the study read in full had 10; all of them measured self-ratings and task scores in a laboratory. No study read asked other people how drunk someone appeared, or tested driving, so none shows how drunk someone looks to others or how they would drive.
claims.magnitude: No effect size is reported for rated drunkenness. Pennings et al. (2002), second-hand: slight decrease in rated drunkenness with cocaine in three studies (Farre 1993, 9 people; Higgins 1993, 8; Farre 1997, 8; Table 1 labels the Farre falls non-significant) and no effect in one (Perez-Reyes and Jeffcoat 1992, 11); rated cocaine high or global intoxication greater with alcohol before or with cocaine in six studies (the review's list includes McCance-Katz et al. 1998, in which any high was short of significance, p = .09); blood alcohol unchanged in one study and about 10% lower, non-significantly, in four; alcohol-induced deficits lessened by cocaine in digit-symbol substitution, sedation, and learning and psychomotor performance; 21 of 600 fatally injured drivers in Los Angeles County and 12 of 285 in Spain positive for both drugs. McCance-Katz et al. (1998): plasma alcohol 99 (SE 7) against 118 (10) mg/dL 90 minutes into the session, p = .008; no drunkenness rating reported. Harris et al. (2003), 10 adults, alcohol 1 g/kg an hour before intravenous cocaine: ratings of alcohol intoxication peaked 55 minutes after the first drink and did not differ between treatments; mean peak breath alcohol at least 0.12 (SD 0.014) g/dL in every condition with alcohol. The same study reports higher ratings of total intoxication and drug liking across time with alcohol than with cocaine alone in 6 of the 10 people, in an unblinded session; it reports no rating of drunkenness separate from the alcohol-intoxication rating.
